The first-stop squeal pattern you're describing is textbook wear-indicator behavior. Here's what's likely happening with your M550i's brakes:

The wear-indicator system. BMW brakes come equipped with a small metal tab on the inner brake pad that's designed to contact the rotor when pad thickness drops below a certain threshold. That contact produces exactly the sound you're hearing — a high-pitched squealing or scraping that's most noticeable on the first braking action of the day or after the car has been sitting. It quiets down after the initial stop because, once the brakes warm up slightly and the pad settles fully into the rotor surface, the tab backs off the contact point.

Why this matters for your situation. Your brake-service record shows work done about 2 months ago, which puts you in that interesting window where wear indicators are starting to activate — pads don't wear linearly, and the first ~500–1,000 miles after a brake service often feels quiet before the indicator starts its job. The ~3 weeks you've been hearing this suggests the pads are now in the zone where the tab is engaging regularly.

The context on your M550i specifically. The 5 Series M550i uses high-performance brake components — larger rotors and pad materials that are engineered for sport driving. These pads tend to wear a bit faster than economy-grade stuff because they're designed for better bite under load, especially on a car this size and power level. You're around 48,500 miles remaining on the brakes before the system flags them as overdue, but the wear-indicator sound is your heads-up that pad thickness is declining. That remaining-mileage estimate assumes "average" driving; spirited driving, a lot of city stop-and-go, or towing would accelerate wear.

What happens next. The squeal is annoying but not urgent — it's your brake system doing its job to alert you. However, you won't want to ignore it for months. Brake Pad Replacement is the straightforward fix here. A shop will pull the wheels, inspect the rotors for scoring or glazing (common when pads run thin), replace the pads and sometimes refresh the rotors, and you'll be quiet and safe again. Because your last service was recent, the odds of needing rotor replacement are lower — but a tech will confirm that when they have the wheels off.
